Why, that suggestion could furnish us with a most exciting superstition. I suppose you will name the insect scarabæus caput hominis, or something similar; the Natural Histories contain plenty of such appellations. But what has become of the antennæ you mentioned?”

“The antennæ!” exclaimed Legrand, growing, for no reason I could understand, rather heated over the matter. “Surely you can see the antennæ. I drew them quite as plainly as they appear on the insect itself, which I should think sufficient.”

“Well, well,” I answered, “perhaps you did; nevertheless, I cannot see them.” I returned the paper without another observation, unwilling to provoke him. Yet this turn in the conversation greatly surprised me; his irritation was inexplicable. As for the beetle’s likeness, absolutely no antennæ could be discerned, and the entire drawing certainly bore a striking resemblance to the usual engravings of a death’s-head.

He took the paper with considerable peevishness and began to crumple it, apparently intending to toss it into the fire, when a passing look at the sketch abruptly arrested his attention. One instant his face flushed deeply; the next it became equally pale. For several minutes he remained seated, inspecting the drawing in the closest detail. Finally he rose, picked up a candle from the table, and sat upon a sea-chest in the room’s remotest corner. There he again examined the paper anxiously, turning it every way. Throughout this he said nothing. His behaviour astonished me, but I judged it wiser not to aggravate his increasing moodiness with any remark. Soon he drew a wallet from his coat pocket, carefully put the paper inside, and secured both in a writing-desk, which he locked. His manner now became calmer, though its former enthusiasm had wholly vanished. Still, he appeared less sullen than preoccupied. As the evening passed, he sank deeper into reflection, and none of my lively remarks could recall his attention. I had meant to spend the night in the hut, as I often had before; but with my host in this state, I thought it best to leave. He made no attempt to detain me, though at our parting he shook my hand with more than his customary warmth.

About a month later, during which time I had not seen Legrand, his servant Jupiter came to visit me in Charleston. Never had I seen the good old Black man so downcast, and I was afraid that some grave misfortune had overtaken my friend.

Yet even then I had not swallowed the last of that bitter draught. I was not fully convinced of my loss; I did not yet feel in every heartbeat, every nerve, every thought, that I alone remained of my race—that I was the last man.

Clouds had gathered during the day, and at sunset a fine rain began to fall. Even the everlasting heavens weep, I thought; why should a mortal man be ashamed to exhaust himself in tears? I recalled the ancient stories in which human beings dissolve through weeping into fountains that flow forever. If only it could be so! Then my fate would share something with the drowning deaths of Adrian and Clara. How strange grief is! From every shape and change around it, grief weaves a fabric on which to record its sorrow. It merges with all living nature and draws nourishment from every object. Like light, it enters everything; like light, it gives everything its own colours.

My search had taken me some distance from the place where I had washed ashore, and I reached one of the watchtowers spaced along the Italian coast. I welcomed the shelter, glad to discover something made by human hands after gazing so long at nature’s desolate emptiness. I entered and climbed the rough spiral staircase to the guardroom. Fate was merciful enough to have left no distressing trace of its former occupants. A few boards resting across two iron trestles and scattered with dried corn leaves offered me a bed. An open chest containing some half-mouldy biscuits awakened an appetite that perhaps had already existed, though I had not noticed it until now. I was also tormented by fierce, parching thirst, caused by the seawater I had swallowed and my body’s exhaustion. Kindly nature had made the satisfaction of these needs a source of pleasure, so that I—even I!—felt refreshed and soothed as I ate this wretched food and drank a little sour wine from a half-full flask left in the deserted tower. Then I lay down on the bed, which a shipwrecked man had no reason to despise. After the hateful smell of seaweed, the earthy scent of the dried leaves comforted my senses. I forgot my loneliness. I looked neither into the past nor toward the future; my senses settled into quiet. I fell asleep and dreamed of beloved inland scenes: haymakers, the shepherd whistling for his dog to help drive the flock into its pen, and the sights and sounds of my mountain childhood that I had long forgotten.

“Well, that’s how everybody lives, Huck.”

“Tom, that makes no difference. I’m not everybody, and I can’t stand it. Being tied down like that is awful. And food comes too easily—I lose interest in eating when it’s like that. I have to ask before I go fishing, ask before I go swimming—damn it, I have to ask before I do anything. And I had to speak so nicely I couldn’t enjoy myself. Every day I had to go up to the attic and swear for a while, just to get the taste of it in my mouth, or I’d have died, Tom. The widow wouldn’t let me smoke or shout or yawn or stretch or scratch in front of people—” Then, with a burst of particular outrage and resentment: “And damn it, she prayed all the time! I’ve never seen a woman like her! I had to leave, Tom. I simply had to. Besides, school’s about to open, and I’d have had to go. Well, I wouldn’t put up with that, Tom. Listen, being rich isn’t what people say it is. It’s nothing but worrying and sweating and wishing you were dead all the time. These clothes suit me, and this barrel suits me, and I’m never giving them up again. Tom, none of this trouble would have happened without that money. Take my share along with yours and give me ten cents now and then—not too often, because I don’t care a damn about anything unless it’s fairly hard to get. And go ask the widow to let me off.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t. It wouldn’t be fair. Besides, if you give it a little longer, you’ll start to like it.”

“Like it! Sure—the way I’d like sitting on a hot stove if I stayed there long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in those damned suffocating houses. I like woods and rivers and big barrels, and I’m sticking with them. Damn everything! Just when we’d got guns and a cave and everything ready for robbing, this stupid business had to happen and spoil it all!”

Tom recognized his chance.

“Listen, Huck, being rich isn’t going to stop me becoming a robber.”

“No! Oh, that’s wonderful! Are you absolutely serious, Tom?”

“As serious as I am sitting here. But Huck, you know we can’t let you join the gang unless you’re respectable.”

Huck’s delight vanished.
